sections.html:
Batavia sits along the Fox River in the western Chicago suburbs, mostly in Kane County with a part in DuPage. The 2020 count was 26,098 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 26,586, up 0.3%. Land area is 10.62 square miles.

Residents tend to stay put: 91.3% of people aged one and over were in the same home a year earlier. Vacancy touched 4.0% of the 10,381 housing units in 2020, with rates of 0.9% for owned homes and 6.2% for rentals.

sections.h2: The Windmill City and its oldest blocks
sections.html:
Settlers arrived in 1833, which makes Batavia the oldest city in Kane County, and incorporation followed on July 27, 1872. Six windmill manufacturers operated here before 1900. Many of the limestone factory buildings still stand and now serve as government and commercial offices and storefronts.

The river and the factory district shaped the oldest part of town, so a Batavia price starts with the block. If your house is within walking distance of the river paths or the old factory district, say so in the first line of the description. If it sits closer to Randall Road, lead with the road access instead.

Batavia Public School District 101 has six K-5 elementary schools, one 6-8 middle school and Batavia High School. Small pockets of the city belong to Geneva Community Unit School District 304 and to West Aurora District 129. The district line can follow a street instead of a city boundary, so confirm the school assignment for your address before you repeat a school claim in a listing.

Batavia Avenue is Illinois Route 31, Main Street is Route 10 and Washington and River streets carry Illinois Route 25 along the river. Randall Road and Wilson Street are also major streets. Pace runs some bus service, and the Geneva and Aurora Metra stations are nearby. The mean commute is 28.9 minutes, and a buyer who commutes by train will ask how far the house is from the nearest platform.

  • Check your house's distance to Route 31 or Randall Road, since buyers weigh traffic and access.
  • Mention river-path access if it is within walking distance.

sections.h2: Which county handles my deed and property record?
sections.html:
Most of the city is in Kane County, whose offices are at 719 Batavia Avenue, Building A, in Geneva, open weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30 with some offices keeping other hours. A portion of Batavia is in DuPage County, so check the parcel number on your tax bill to see which recorder and treasurer apply.

Illinois transfer tax is paid with stamps the recorder sells, and both parties sign Form PTAX-203 for the county. Home rule municipalities may levy extra, so ask the title company whether Batavia does. For recording charges, contact your county's recorder.

Whichever way you sell, the paperwork looks the same. The deed has to name every owner, any lender must be paid off from the proceeds, and the recorder in the parcel's county files the transfer. A parcel in the DuPage portion follows a different office than one in the Kane portion.

  • Confirm the county from the parcel number.
  • Ask the title company for a payoff figure and a list of every charge, including any home rule tax.
  • Sign Form PTAX-203 along with the deed.
  • Ask for a copy of the recorded deed once the county returns it.

sections.h2: When selling for cash makes sense
sections.html:
Selling for cash as-is fits a house with tired systems, a property from an estate, or an owner with a fixed moving date. A listing fits a house in show-ready shape. The trade is speed and certainty against the price a fully updated house might reach.

  • Ask for the offer in writing and set it beside the net from a listing after repairs and fees.
  • Confirm how quickly the buyer can close and who covers title and recording.
  • Gather your tax bill, payoff letter and permit records before the title company asks.

Plenty of Batavia buyers take houses in their current state, and a cash offer reflects the condition. You do not have to repair first, but you should know what is open at your address so the written terms match reality.

sections.h2: Preparing the house and the paperwork
sections.html:
Older houses near the river and the old factory district tend to raise inspection questions about wiring, roofs and basements. Collect receipts for any work you have done and the permit records for additions or remodels. A seller who can show dates and invoices gives buyers less to argue about, whether the offer is cash or financed.

Because Batavia sits in two counties, line up the documents in the right office from the start. The county printed on your tax bill tells you where the deed gets recorded and who collects the tax. Then settle the current year's tax and any open installment through the title company so the closing statement shows a clear balance.

sections.h2: A step-by-step path for a Batavia seller
sections.html:
Selling goes faster when the steps are in order. Begin with the parcel number on your tax bill and learn whether the house is in the Kane or DuPage part of the city. Next, decide between a listing, a private sale and a cash buyer. Then collect the papers a buyer or title company will request: the tax bill, a payoff letter from any lender, and permit records.

When a contract is signed, the title company runs the search and prepares the closing statement. The deed has to name every owner, so if the house passed through an estate or a family transfer, tell the title company early and ask what extra documents the recorder needs. At closing, the lender is paid from the proceeds, the seller receives the balance, and the county recorder files the deed. Ask for the recorded copy and keep it with your closing papers.

sections.h2: What buyers want to know about a Batavia address
sections.html:
Buyers ask three things first: which county, which school district and how far the house is from the main roads or the train. Having those answers ready saves time. Write the district into the listing only after you have checked the street, since boundaries can follow a road. Say whether the river path or the old downtown is a short walk. For a house that needs work, state the condition plainly and let the price carry it.

If an inspector finds old wiring, a worn roof or a damp basement, the cash route keeps those items out of negotiation, while a listing may bring requests for credits or repairs. Neither route is wrong. Pick the one that fits your timeline and how much work you want to take on before closing.

faqs.q: Is my Batavia house in Kane or DuPage County?
faqs.a: Most likely Kane, though part of the city lies in DuPage. The parcel number on your tax bill settles it and tells you which recorder files the deed.
Batavia Public School District 101 covers most of the city, with small areas in Geneva District 304 and West Aurora District 129. Check your address.
The Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, completed by buyer and seller and filed in the county of the parcel as part of the recording.

faqs.q: Do I have to repair before a sale?
faqs.a: No. Many buyers take houses in their current state, and a cash offer reflects the condition. Insist on written terms and weigh the net against a listing.
The sale contract decides. Revenue stamps for the state tax come through the county recorder, and a home rule municipality or county may add its own. Your title company can list each charge.
